questions.title: Newton's law of gravitation & the Earth–Moon neutral point

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: The gravitational force (between two point masses) is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer:
g = F/m.
F = GMm/r², so g = GMm/(mr²) = GM/r²

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: At point X the gravitational fields due to the Earth and the Moon have <u>equal magnitudes</u> and act in <u>opposite directions</u>, so the resultant gravitational field strength is zero.

questions.title: Charged sphere in electric & magnetic fields — circular motion & flux density

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: Vertically downwards.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer: The magnetic force on the sphere is always <u>perpendicular</u> to its velocity, so it provides the centripetal force (centripetal acceleration) and changes the direction but not the speed of the sphere.

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer:
For the sphere to stay at a fixed height the electric force balances the weight: Eq = mg.
E = mg/q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 9.81 / (0.27 × 10⁻⁹) = 5.8 N C⁻¹

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer:
Centripetal force = magnetic force, so Bqv = mv²/r.
B = mv/qr = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.78 / (0.27 × 10⁻⁹ × 3.4) = 0.14 T

questions.title: Ideal gas & first law — pV = nRT, work done & internal energy

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: An ideal gas is a gas that obeys pV ∝ T, where p is the pressure, V is the volume and T is the thermodynamic (absolute) temperature.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer:
Using ΔU = q + W, where W is the work done on the gas:
AB: work = +19.2 kJ, thermal energy = −48.0 kJ, so ΔU = 19.2 − 48.0 = −28.8 kJ.
BC: constant volume so work = 0; the total ΔU over the whole cycle is zero, so ΔU = +28.8 kJ and thermal energy = +28.8 kJ.
CA: isothermal so ΔU = 0; work = −31.6 kJ, so thermal energy = +31.6 kJ.

questions.title: Pendulum — simple harmonic motion, angular frequency & amplitude

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The graph is a straight line through the origin, showing that a is proportional to x, and the gradient is negative, showing that a is in the opposite direction to x.

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: Increasing L decreases ω (since ω = √(k/L)). The total energy E = ½mω²x₀² is constant, so as ω decreases the amplitude x₀ increases.

questions.title: Full-wave rectification — bridge circuit & smoothing capacitor

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: Rectification is the conversion of an alternating current (a.c.) to a direct current (d.c.).

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer: Full-wave rectification.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: P is labelled − (negative) and Q is labelled + (positive).

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer:
Peak voltage V₀ = 6.0 V, so the voltage axis has ticks of 4 V and 8 V at the 2 cm marks (peak at 6.0 V).
T = 2π/ω = 2π/25π = 0.08 s.
The time axis has ticks of 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12 s at the 2 cm marks.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: Capacitor symbol drawn correctly, connected in parallel with the 1.2 kΩ load resistor.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer: Straight lines (or curves) with negative decreasing gradient drawn between adjacent peaks, falling from each peak to meet the rising edge of the next peak, with a drop in p.d. of 1½ small squares (0.6 V).

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.answer:
Minimum smoothed voltage V = 0.90 × 6.0 = 5.4 V, and the discharge time for each half-cycle is 0.034 s.
V = V₀ exp(−t/RC): 5.4 = 6.0 exp[−0.034/(1.2 × 10³ × C)].
ln 0.90 = −0.034/(1.2 × 10³ × C), giving C = 2.7 × 10⁻⁴ F

questions.title: Magnetic flux & induced e.m.f. in a coil

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Magnetic flux is the product of the magnetic flux density and the area, where the area is measured <u>perpendicular</u> to the magnetic field.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
At t = 0.60 s, B = 400 mT (from Fig. 6.2).
Flux linkage = BAN = 400 × 10⁻³ × 0.12² × 8 = 0.046 Wb

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: The graph is a straight line, so B (and hence the flux linkage) changes at a constant rate, giving a constant induced e.m.f.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer: E = rate of change of flux linkage = NΦ/t = 0.046/0.60 = 0.077 V

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: The induced e.m.f. causes a current to flow in the coil. Either: the current in the magnetic field causes forces on the (opposite sides of the) coil, forcing the coil inwards; or: the current dissipates energy in the resistance of the coil, so the temperature of the coil rises.

questions.title: Photoelectric effect — threshold frequency, work function & intensity

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: A photon is a quantum of energy of electromagnetic radiation.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: The photoelectric effect.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer:
Any three:
1. There is a minimum (threshold) frequency below which no electrons are emitted — the threshold frequency is 5.4 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
2. The work function of the metal is 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (2.2 eV) — the intercept on the E_MAX axis.
3. E_MAX increases linearly with frequency.
4. The gradient of the line is the Planck constant (6.7 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: A different metal has a different work function, so the graph has a different threshold frequency (different intercept on the frequency axis) but the same gradient.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer: The photons have the same energy (same frequency), so the maximum kinetic energy E_MAX is unchanged and the line is unchanged. The greater intensity only increases the number of electrons emitted per second (the photocurrent).

questions.title: Nuclear binding energy & fusion energy release

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: Nuclear binding energy is the energy required to separate all the nucleons of a nucleus to infinity.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer: A curve starting close to the origin, rising steeply to a single peak positioned to the left of centre (at small nucleon number A), then falling gently (shallow) on the right-hand side.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: Fusion.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: Both hydrogen-2 and helium-3 have low nucleon numbers, at the left-hand end of the graph, where binding energy per nucleon rises with A. Helium-3 has a higher binding energy per nucleon than hydrogen-2, so the products are more tightly bound and energy is released.

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer:
Δm = (2 × 2.014 102) − (3.016 029 + 1.008 665) = 0.00351 u.
Energy per reaction = Δmc² = 0.00351 × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 5.24 × 10⁻¹³ J.
1.00 mol of deuterium forms 0.500 mol of helium-3, i.e. 0.500 × 6.02 × 10²³ reactions.
Total energy = 0.500 × 6.02 × 10²³ × 5.24 × 10⁻¹³ = 1.58 × 10¹¹ J

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: Electrons are accelerated (by a large applied p.d.) onto a metal target. When the electrons hit the target and decelerate, X-rays are produced.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer: The images of the multiple sections are combined to create a three-dimensional (3-D) image.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
Point P is through 5.6 cm of soft tissue only.
I = I₀ exp(−μx) = I₀ exp(−0.89 × 5.6) = 0.0068 I₀

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer:
Point Q is through 2.4 cm of bone and 3.2 cm of soft tissue.
I = I₀ exp(−3.4 × 2.4) × exp(−0.89 × 3.2) = I₀ exp(−8.16) × exp(−2.848) = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ I₀

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: The detected intensities at P and Q are very different (0.0068 I₀ compared with 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ I₀), so there is a large difference in detected intensity and the image has good contrast.

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The wavelength of maximum intensity (peak wavelength) is <u>inversely proportional</u> to the thermodynamic temperature: λ_MAX ∝ 1/T.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
From Fig. 10.1: λ_MAX = 0.50 μm for star A and 0.65 μm for star B.
λ_MAX T = constant, so T_B = 5800 × (0.50/0.65) = 4500 K

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: Star B has a greater peak (average) wavelength than star A, so star B looks redder than star A.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: Redshift is the increase in the apparent wavelength of light (above its known laboratory value), due to the star moving away from the observer.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer: By examining the lines in the spectrum of light from the star and comparing their positions with the known (laboratory) spectrum, so that the increase in wavelength can be identified.
